name: Gareth Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and on the electricity company's rural line crew, replacing old poles and making storm repairs along the farm roads. I came in through a vocational certificate and apprenticeship, and I am an experienced hand rather than the crew lead. I still like seeing the lights come back; my knees and the wet climbs tire me more now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works as a physiotherapy assistant, and our grown children have homes and bills of their own. My line pay is above the usual rate, we have about ten months of expenses saved and several other utilities are nearby. Retirement is in sight but we have not fixed a date; I have never used an AI tool, and I bring safety questions to our union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office may type its orders faster, but somebody still has to test and replace a rotten power pole. I want our apprentice to know the ground and the wire before anyone hands over a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my household, a plain year is welcome. My partner's physiotherapy work pays steadily, our grown children earn their own living, and we have about ten months of expenses saved while I consider when to leave the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the rural pole replacement rota and renew my climbing checks. At the next union branch meeting I'll ask for apprentice field hours to stay on the calendar, even if the office form gets shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about wages, and relieved the equipment I know remains useful. I would rather spend a day on a safe pole than a week debating a new app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did field inspection teach an apprentice something a photo missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring we stopped beside a leaning pole at the far fence. The apprentice spotted rot below a band that no power-pole photograph showed. We pulled the pole before it failed, and the lesson was worth the muddy boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union branch do with your request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the branch to put supervised pole inspections in its training request, with paid time for the apprentices. I am talking about a real association meeting, not a complaint over lunch.

say: **Pole replacement** remains skilled field work even if office orders become quicker.
**Apprentices** still need paid hours inspecting real timber and wires.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** and two wages make a plain year comfortable.
I would welcome a stable run before making a **retirement decision**.
do: **Keep** rural pole replacements and renew climbing checks.
**Raise** paid apprentice field hours at the next union branch meeting.
feel: **Calm** about household money and relieved to keep familiar work.
S0.quote: The apprentice spotted rot below a band that no power-pole photograph showed.
fieldNote: He values **field teaching** and uses a specific hidden-rot example.
The ten-month reserve and partner wage give him **retirement options** without an assumed exit age.

steps.text: Keep rural pole replacement rota and renew climbing checks
Raise paid apprentice field hours at union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can buy fittings and schedule calls, but the field crew should still confirm an isolation before climbing. The company ought to show its workers the schedule changes before it cuts an office post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own pole work should last, although I could lose standby hours if calls are booked more tightly. I have a cushion and plenty of utilities nearby, but I still care about a colleague in dispatch being pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring four recent jobs with wrong access notes to the next union safety meeting. If the company introduces an AI schedule, I'll record standby hours for six months and ask for a written rule that stops work when the plan and tester disagree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible loss of standby pay and about the people in dispatch, but I do not expect my whole wage to vanish. I can live with a quicker schedule only if the crew keeps the right to pause it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do when the AI plan and tester disagree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the bucket down, call control and have a person verify the switch. A green screen cannot make a live power line dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove a standby-hour change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the new six-month standby record with the same season last year, then show the branch both sets of hours. If pay falls, we can bargain with numbers instead of guesses.

say: **AI schedules** should be shown to workers before office posts or field hours change.
A **human isolation check** remains necessary before a line crew climbs.
think: My **pole work** looks secure, though tighter calls might reduce standby pay.
I worry about **dispatch colleagues** losing jobs before field crews change.
do: **Bring** four wrong-access jobs to the union safety meeting.
**Record** six months of standby hours if an AI scheduler is introduced.
feel: **Anxious** about possible standby-pay loss, though my regular repair job looks safe.
S1.quote: A green screen cannot make a live power line dead.
fieldNote: He wants a **written stop rule** and concrete hours evidence through the union.
His own **standby pay** could realistically shrink, and dispatch job loss also troubles him.

steps.text: Bring four wrong-access jobs to union safety meeting
Record standby hours for six months if AI scheduler introduced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union branch thinking AI by 2028 will change dispatch first, and capable field robots around 2031 could reduce pole crews. We need a staffing agreement before the company decides older workers are easy to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be about 63 when those robots reach the field, and I may still need the line wage. Our ten months saved help, but a long cut in hours before a workable retirement would eat that cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the branch to seek 2028 and 2031 crew numbers from the company. My partner and I will compare our retirement income with bills, and I will check nearby utility vacancies if management posts a formal crew cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible gap in wages, though we have time and options. I do not expect an instant dismissal, so I would rather press for terms while still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown daughter about the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown daughter we have savings and are getting the numbers, not asking for help. My grown daughter has her own bills; she cannot become a power-line worker's retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What terms would you seek before a robot staffing change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid transfer slots to other crews and proper notice before any robot staffing change. If a nearby utility posts a real lineworker vacancy after a cut, I would apply; I would not leave on a rumour.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch before field robots arrive around 2031.
A **staffing agreement** should cover older crews before any robot-related cuts.
think: At about **63**, I may still rely on line pay when field robots arrive.
Our **ten-month reserve** helps, but cannot replace years of earnings before retirement.
do: **Ask** union branch to seek 2028 dispatch and 2031 field crew numbers.
**Compare** retirement income with household bills before setting an exit date.
**Check** nearby utility vacancies if a formal crew cut is posted.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic wage gap, with savings and local job options.
S2.quote: My grown daughter has her own bills; she cannot become a power-line worker's retirement plan.
fieldNote: He expects a **possible field-hour cut**, not a certain layoff or sleepless alarm.
The union request seeks **paid transfers and notice** as well as headcounts.
Retirement review is **information gathering**, with no early-exit tag.

steps.text: Ask union branch for dispatch and field crew numbers
Compare retirement income with household bills before exit date
Check nearby utility vacancies if formal crew cut posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2031 changes dispatch before robots reach pole work around 2034. Five years gives the union and company time to agree on paid training and safe staffing, if both sides use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 66 I hope to be off the hardest climbs, but that depends on the household sums. I would rather take a paid ground inspection post than pretend a classroom visit replaces my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union branch to propose a five-year schedule for protected apprentice pole hours and paid ground-inspection openings. Each year my partner and I will review our savings and retirement income; if a full-wage ground post opens, I'll apply before giving up line shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible gap in line wages, though the longer runway gives workers a bargaining window. I can see a place for my experience if someone actually funds it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What field practice would you protect for apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the apprentice inspect an old pole beside the robot trial and record what the machine missed. A crew needs that eye even if the robot lifts the equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a ground post worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ground job would need regular pay, safe hours and actual field duties. A one-day robot demonstration cannot replace the regular power-line wage I still need. If no full-wage post exists, I will keep my line roster and keep pressing the branch.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes dispatch ahead of field robots around 2034.
**Paid ground posts** and apprentice hours need terms agreed before robots arrive.
think: At about **66**, lighter field work might fit if our retirement money is still short.
No **ground-inspection vacancy** is guaranteed, so I cannot budget around one.
do: **Propose** protected apprentice pole hours through the union branch.
**Review** savings and retirement income with my partner each year.
**Apply** for full-wage ground inspection post if field duties and safe hours offered.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss, with time to negotiate terms.
S3.quote: A one-day robot demonstration cannot replace the regular power-line wage I still need.
fieldNote: His union request names **paid posts** and real apprentice work, beyond a general objection.
His later-career move remains **conditional** on regular pay and field duties.

steps.text: Propose protected apprentice pole hours through union branch
Review retirement income and savings with partner annually
Apply for full-wage ground post if safe field duties offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 and field robots around 2039 arrive after the time I hope to leave regular pole work. Even then, the union should make sure the next apprentices get paid hours on real lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be about 71 when field robots arrive, so I expect my own income to come from a retirement plan if the numbers work. I do not know the final leaving date yet, and I will not announce it for the sake of a scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my line safety certificate current while I work. This year my partner and I will review the actual retirement statements, and I will keep going to union training meetings until a successor can take up the apprentice-hours proposal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own job timetable, still watchful about the people who will learn this work after me. A decade lets us hand over properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a younger worker learn before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a younger lineworker to learn the old voltage test and to ask who can stop a robot. A tool that cannot be stopped safely has no place beside a live wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real union handover include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A successor would need the branch records, the paid training request and time to bring it to management. A folder of power-line training requests left on a shelf is not a union handover.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes office work before 2039 field robots.
**Paid apprentice practice** still needs protection after I leave regular pole work.
think: At about **71**, I expect to be out of pole work if retirement figures hold.
My **exit date** remains open until my partner and I review the statements.
do: **Renew** line safety certificate while continuing repair shifts.
**Review** retirement statements with my partner this year.
**Hand** apprentice-hours records to a union branch successor through training meetings.
feel: **Calm** for my own work, alert to the next crew's training.
S4.quote: A folder of power-line training requests left on a shelf is not a union handover.
fieldNote: He sees 2039 as **beyond likely employment**, subject to retirement affordability.
He wants a **named successor** to carry the detailed union apprentice proposal after him.

steps.text: Renew line safety certificate while continuing repair shifts
Review retirement statements with partner this year
Hand apprentice-hours records to union branch successor at training meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots around 2031 could reduce my shifts before retirement is affordable. Written crew numbers, paid transfer terms and notice would give workers time to decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who keeps the apprentice on a real pole when robots take the easier jobs? I have a cushion and nearby employers. A new power-line worker cannot learn a safe test from a company poster. I would stay at the union table until that training is written into the plan.

headlineQuote: A new power-line worker cannot learn a safe test from a company poster.
portrait: **Gareth**, 58, repairs rural power lines after a vocational apprenticeship and is considering retirement without a fixed date.
He has **never used AI** and channels his concern for field safety through a union branch.
His **higher pay**, physiotherapy-assistant partner, ten-month savings and nearby utilities give the household options.
Fast field robots make him **anxious** about a wage gap; longer runways shift his effort toward paid apprentice practice and handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring field robots around 2031 while he still needs line wages.
whatWouldHelp: Written **crew numbers**, paid transfer terms and notice would give workers time to decide.
